transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-09-10 09:00 PT
Duration: 1:18
Attendees: Asha, Miguel, Lena, Ben, Priya, Zahid, Tom, Grace

Summary: Quick internal field enablement to test out refreshed messaging hypotheses on cost/latency tradeoffs, competitive differentiators, and demo playbooks. Run two short roleplays, capture alternative rebuttals, and decide final one-pager updates.

Topics: messaging anchors, competitive positioning vs Anthropic/OpenAI, demo scripts for streaming and fallback, security blurbs for SOC2/KMS, roleplay scenarios.

[00:00] Asha Rao: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to keep this tight, about an hour, we'll run through the new messaging, then do two roleplays and assign next steps.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Awesome. I have my notepad, I'm hoping we can get a short one-liner that works for both mid-market and enterprise.
[00:28] Miguel Torres: Cool, I'll kick off with the demo framing — remember the ask: make latency/cost tangible for AEs, 90 second elevator.
[00:38] Zahid Khan: Quick timezone check — EMEA friendly, thanks.
[00:45] Asha Rao: Great. Lena, can you start with the new messaging bullets?
[00:50] Lena Park: Yep. So hypothesis one: "Predictable inference economics, not just model access." We lead with cost per 1k tokens and the levers — batching, KV cache, quantization. Phrase idea: 'Same API, smarter serving'.
[01:12] Tom Li: When we say KV cache to customers, some AEs get blank stares — we should use prefix cache or warm cache language maybe.
[01:25] Miguel Torres: Good call. ASR note: sometimes KV cache gets transcribed as K V cash in demo notes, haha.
[01:33] Ben Carter: Also highlight Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoff: predictable throughput for Reserved, best TCO in sustained workloads.
[01:42] Grace Huang: For trainers, shorter concrete examples help: "X company saved Y% by enabling prefix cache and switching to 4-bit quantized variant." Even if approximate, gives field mental anchor.
[01:58] Asha Rao: Ok let's try a one-liner swap exercise. I'll read a version, then Priya you'll roleplay an AE trying to qualify for latency-sensitive use case.
[02:08] Asha Rao: "Redwood gives you a single inference API that makes large-model performance predictable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — so you can scale without surprise bills or late nights."
[02:25] Priya Nair: Hmm, I like the predictability part. I worry 'late nights' might land differently with enterprise folks. Could maybe say 'surprise bills or operational headaches' — more neutral.
[02:40] Zahid Khan: For EMEA, 'surprise bills' resonates, but keep it slightly more formal.
[02:47] Miguel Torres: Technical anchor we can add after the one-liner: "We lower per-token cost via workload-aware batching and intelligent caching, and we offer reserved capacity for predictable tail latency."
[02:59] Tom Li: Can we practice that as a two-sentence skit? People need to hear it.
[03:06] [03:06] Roleplay 1 start — Priya as AE, Miguel as SE (speaker overlap, slight crosstalk)
[03:10] Priya (AE): We're building a live chat agent for our support app — sub-200ms p95 is a hard req. How does Redwood help?
[03:18] Miguel (SE): Great question. Short answer: we provide reserved GPU pools and routing policies that prioritize low latency; on the hosting side we also support pre-warmed KV cache and streaming so the p95 drops into your SLO band.
[03:36] Priya (AE): What about cost though — my CFO will ask.
[03:40] Miguel (SE): Right — so we show two concrete levers: reserved capacity for consistent tail latency and automatic batching for bursty query patterns to lower per-token cost. For example, in a support bot pilot we saw a 30% token-cost reduction when combining prefix caching and an optimized batch size.
[03:58] Priya (AE): That sounds good. Any risk to model quality with batching/quantization?
[04:03] Miguel (SE): Minor quality delta — we recommend running a short eval suite (we help with the eval harness) to pick the quantization profile. Also fallback routing can send critical queries to a higher-fidelity model when needed.
[04:20] [04:20] Asha: Small note — when we say 'quantization profile' to sales, use 'model compression profile' first and tier up from there.
[04:29] Grace: Noted.
[04:32] [04:32] Roleplay ends. Quick debrief.
[04:35] Priya: That felt natural. I had one sticky point — 'fallback routing' needs a one-liner.
[04:40] Ben: Suggestion: 'automatic fallback to higher fidelity only on edge cases, so most traffic gets the cheaper path'.
[04:48] Miguel: Also add 'transparent audit logs and KMS integration' — security hooks sell in enterprise.
[04:55] Zahid: On security, some folks ask specifically for SOC 2 and KMS, and also VPC peering or on-prem. We should have that as a succinct paragraph in the one-pager.
[05:06] Lena: We'll create a 'security blurb' paragraph: SOC 2 Type II, optional customer-managed KMS, VPC/private deployment options with audit log examples.
[05:18] [05:18] Asha: Ok second section: competitor positioning. Who wants to read the list?
[05:22] Tom: I'll take it. First competitor shorthand: Anthropic — model quality lever, but typically higher cost for comparable latency.
[05:31] Tom: OpenAI — great model access but less focus on dedicated infra and predictable tail latency, also limited private deploy options for some customers.
[05:44] Priya: Vertex — strong for Google Cloud-native shops, but lacks our cross-deployment rollout/control plane granularity.
[05:57] Miguel: Add note: some customers will say they self-host — rebut: self-host requires deep ops into kernel tuning and continual performance investment; we offer the same controls with less operational drag.
[06:15] [06:15] Asha: Let’s practice a competitive objection: 'Why not just go to OpenAI for simplicity'? Zahid, you're on.
[06:21] Zahid Khan: Ok. 'We're a startup; OpenAI is easy and cheaper to start.'
[06:26] Miguel: Rebuttal: 'OpenAI is great for experimentation. For scale, Redwood helps you predict spend and keep latency SLOs, plus dedicated options to keep customer data under your control — which matters for compliance.'
[06:45] Zahid: That landed well. Also mention our pricing model — usage-based but with reserved tiers.
[06:52] Asha: Good. Next: demo flow tweaks. Miguel, show the two demo sequences you want the field to run.
[06:59] Miguel: Sure. Sequence A: Hosted fast path demo. Start with quick prompt, show streaming tokens, demonstrate latency live, then show cost estimate panel. Sequence B: Failure mode + fallback — intentionally introduce long context to trigger fallback to dedicated variant, show routing and audit log entries.
[07:25] Tom: For Sequence B, ensure you don't sound like you 'break' the demo — phrase it as 'stress test' or 'edge-case route'.
[07:33] Miguel: Noted. We'll practice the exact script.
[07:37] [07:37] Demo dry run (abbreviated audio transcript markers)
[07:40] Miguel (screen share): Starting the streaming example — prompt sent, tokens streaming... p50 45ms, p95 120ms in this sandbox. Cost panel shows estimated 0.0004 USD/token (note: sandbox pricing).
[08:05] Priya: Can you comment on different hardware footprints? Like A10 vs A100?
[08:10] Miguel: Yes — hardware affects kernel selection and max throughput. We recommend A100s for high throughput sustained inference; lower-cost GPUs with optimized kernels for mid-tier. We'll add a short appendix in the playbook.
[08:24] [08:24] Asha: Quick objection workshop — split into two groups. Group one: cost-sensitive buyer; group two: latency-sensitive buyer. We'll roleplay 5 minutes each.
[08:36] [08:36] Roleplay 2 start — Grace as buyer (cost), Ben as AE.
[08:40] Grace (buyer): Our CFO is focused on monthly burn — how do you convince him?
[08:45] Ben (AE): We lead with 'predictable economics' and show a model of projected tokens per month, then show savings with batching/caching, call out reserved capacity commit options for predictable pricing.
[08:58] Grace: What about hidden costs — infra ops?
[09:02] Ben: That's a valid concern; we position Redwood as removing engineering ops for serving — we handle runtime, kernel tuning, and offer private deployment if you need on-prem, but we still manage the compilation and serving runtime for you.
[09:18] [09:18] Debrief — group swap notes.
[09:22] Priya: Two quick field notes: 1) AEs want the 'one-liner' and 'data point' up front, 2) SEs want a short demo clip they can forward after calls.
[09:32] Miguel: We'll prioritize a 90-second demo clip showing streaming + fallback.
[09:36] [09:36] Interruptions and misc chatter — microphone tests, people joining late.
[10:02] Zahid: I have a question on rollout policies — can we do canary to 10% and fallback to host?
[10:08] Miguel: Yes, rollout policies support canary/A B test, with automatic fallback to a compatible variant if the canary exceeds error thresholds. We'll document default thresholds in the ops playbook.
[10:21] Lena: Also add a short table with recommended thresholds and monitoring signals.
[10:26] Tom: Another ask from field: sample eval sets for chatbots vs embeddings workloads.
[10:33] Miguel: We'll surface two repo examples and a short notebook; reuse the evaluation harness from the onboarding repo.
[10:40] [10:40] Quick pause — small audio glitch, transcript slightly corrupted here. Speaker labels may switch.
[11:01] Asha: Let's capture the final one-pager structure: 1) one-line value prop; 2) three bullets (predictable economics, deployment flexibility, security); 3) 2-3 quick data points; 4) 3 common objections + rebuttals; 5) two demo scripts + link to 90s clip.
[11:25] Priya: For the 2-3 data points, use range language: 'pilot customers see 20-40% token cost reduction depending on workload.' Avoid claiming a single number.
[11:36] Ben: Action: create a slide with that layout and share by Friday.
[11:40] [11:40] Short brainstorm on objection wording.
[11:45] Grace: Rebuttal phrasing for 'we'll self-host' — 'self-host gives you control, but often at high ops cost; Redwood shortens time-to-value and offers private deployment if you need full control.'
[11:58] Zahid: It helps to show a small TCO table comparing self-host vs Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated over 12 months.
[12:04] Miguel: We'll mock a sample TCO with simple assumptions and leave it editable for AEs.
[12:12] [12:12] Final roleplay — Zahid as AE, Miguel as skeptical engineering buyer.
[12:16] Zahid (AE): We're seeing latency spikes at scale; engineering is worried about rework.
[12:22] Miguel (SE): We do kernel selection, autoscaling, and we can pin model versions for rollouts; migration path includes a pilot with canary and rollback hooks.
[12:34] Zahid: Ok, what do we hand to engineering?
[12:38] Miguel: A short runbook: deployment architecture diagram, KMS integration notes, audit log examples, and p95 targets for reserved tiers. We'll attach that to the pilot checklist.
[12:52] Asha: Great. We're at about 40 minutes in — timecheck. Two more logistical items: CRM copy and collateral links.
[13:02] Ben: CRM copy should be a short paragraph and a checklist fields: pilot objective, success criteria, stakeholders, and timeline. We'll provide a template.
[13:13] Lena: Collateral links — I'll attach a folder with one-pager, demo clip, security blurb, TCO spreadsheet.
[13:23] Priya: One last quick objection: 'What about model drift and quality regression with quantization?'
[13:29] Miguel: We set up continuous evals against a prompt set and alert on regression. Also canary first then roll out quantized variants gradually.
[13:40] [13:40] Wrap — recap and explicit next steps readout.
[13:43] Asha: Recap: Lena to update one-pager and security blurb; Miguel record demo clips and TCO mock; Asha send pilot checklist and pricing matrix; Grace/Ben incorporate into trainer deck and schedule follow-up roleplay.
[13:58] Priya: I'll run the subject-line A/B test with my accounts and report back.
[14:05] Zahid: I'll coordinate an EMEA session in local hours.
[14:10] Asha: Thanks everyone — we'll reconvene after materials are in flight.
[14:15] [14:15] Meeting ends.

Notes on transcript quality: some speaker labels and exact timings are approximate, a few words transcribed incorrectly (e.g., K V cash instead of KV cache), occasional dropped words during demo screen-share segments.
